items.title: Utilities are starting to triage which AI data centers actually get grid access
items.summary: Drawing on planning filings from Georgia Power, Duke Energy, and Dominion Energy, Data Center Knowledge outlines how utilities are beginning to decide which AI data-center projects actually get connected. The documents show utilities screening large-load requests, testing demand scenarios, and sequencing infrastructure investment rather than treating every announced campus as firm demand. What emerges is an early, still-uneven framework for rationing scarce grid capacity among competing gigawatt-scale requests.
items.whyItMatters: As large-load requests pile up faster than utilities can build, not every announced data center will secure timely interconnection. Understanding the criteria utilities apply — load certainty, creditworthiness, and system impact — helps developers position projects and helps analysts separate speculative announcements from the campuses most likely to be built.

corroboratingSources.label: DOE data center electricity demand report

items.title: Hyperscale AI loads are rewriting the utility planning playbook
items.summary: Data Center Knowledge reports that hyperscale AI campuses are pushing utilities, grid operators, and developers to rethink long-standing planning assumptions. Interviewees describe compressing transmission, interconnection, and reliability timelines to keep pace with demand that is arriving faster and at larger scale than traditional forecasts anticipated. The piece frames AI load as a structural break from the incremental growth utilities are accustomed to planning around.
items.whyItMatters: If legacy planning models understate how quickly and how large AI load can appear, utilities risk falling behind on transmission and generation. For developers, the practical lesson is that securing grid access increasingly depends on engaging early with utility planning cycles rather than assuming capacity will be available on request.

corroboratingSources.label: EIA: Commercial electricity sales soar in Virginia

items.title: Virginia's commercial power demand has surged on data-center growth, EIA data shows
items.summary: According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Annual Electric Power Industry Report, commercial-sector electricity sales in Virginia rose by nearly 30 million megawatthours between 2019 and 2025. Only Texas — a far larger state — added more commercial demand over the same period. EIA links the increase largely to the state's dense concentration of data centers, whose server load is captured in the commercial category.
items.whyItMatters: Virginia is the clearest real-world signal of how quickly a data-center cluster can reshape a state's load profile. The pace of this growth underscores why utilities in the 'Data Center Alley' corridor are racing to expand generation, transmission, and interconnection capacity, and it offers a concrete demand benchmark for other states courting similar development.
